concepts.supporting_text: This led to the development of models that used relationships between the oceans, atmosphere, sea ice and land surfaces to improve understanding of climate change over time.

concepts.name: Green movement

concepts.name: Precautionary principle

concepts.name: Substantial equivalence

concepts.name: Pseudo scientific concepts

concepts.supporting_text: In circumstances of scientific uncertainty, policy makers introduce 'pseudo' scientific concepts to support their decisions.

concepts.name: Frankenfoods

concepts.name: Scientific authority
concepts.definition: The power and influence of scientific expertise to shape societal understanding of environmental issues, which can be exaggerated, dramatized, or oversimplified and is contested by various interest groups.

concepts.name: Trust in individuals and institutions

concepts.name: Burden of proof

concepts.name: Environmental campaign groups
concepts.definition: Organised collectives that employ scientific expertise to diagnose environmental problems and use that evidence in legal actions, petitions, and public advocacy to influence policy and corporate behavior.

concepts.name: Scientific consensus (IPCC reports)

concepts.name: Climate scepticism

concepts.name: IPCC peer-review process

concepts.name: Public relations disaster (CRU email leak)

concepts.name: environmental economics
concepts.definition: A relatively undeveloped field that attempts to outline environmental constraints to the economic system and to move away from a focus on economic growth, while also developing ways of ensuring environmental interests are reflected in the market economy.

concepts.name: economic value of the environment

concepts.supporting_text: Over the past half‑century, the development of concepts and theories that recognise the economic value of the environment has become increasingly central to the environmental cause.

concepts.name: environmental constraints to the economic system

concepts.supporting_text: a series of academics have attempted to outline environmental constraints to the economic system and to move away from the focus on economic growth.

concepts.name: greener economic system

concepts.supporting_text: Meanwhile, the ongoing global economic crisis has provided real opportunities for environmentalists to promote a greener economic system.

concepts.name: public trust in science
concepts.definition: The confidence that the public places in scientific evidence and its use by the environmental movement, which has been eroded and needs to be rebuilt to support effective campaigning.
concepts.supporting_text: The challenge for the environmental movement is to rebuild public trust in the way it uses science to support arguments in order to take action to address environmental issues.

concepts.name: environmental agenda
concepts.definition: The set of priorities and actions driven by scientific understanding of environmental problems and solutions, shaping policy and public opinion over the past fifty years.
concepts.supporting_text: Over the past fifty years, science has driven the environmental agenda, explaining the cause and impact of environmental problems and the implications they have for society as a whole.

concepts.name: Law of diminishing returns
concepts.definition: A principle in agriculture stating that there is a maximum point of land productivity that cannot be surpassed, implying that the amount of available land limits population and wealth.
concepts.supporting_text: Anne‑Robert‑Jacques Turgot (1727‑81) outlined a law of diminishing returns in agriculture, arguing that there was a maximum point of land productivity that was impossible to surpass.

concepts.name: Malthusian principle
concepts.definition: The idea that population growth, initially driven by surplus food production, will eventually be constrained by limits to productive land and a resultant shortage of food, putting society under permanent threat of starvation unless population expansion is limited.
concepts.supporting_text: An idea forcefully argued by Thomas Malthus (1766‑1834) … Malthus explained that population growth, driven initially by surplus food production, would eventually be constrained by limits to productive land and a resultant shortage of food.

concepts.name: Stationary state economy
concepts.definition: An economic vision in which unlimited economic growth is avoided, emphasizing the preservation of natural environments and warning against the exhaustive transformation of land and wildlife for human use.
concepts.supporting_text: John Stuart Mill … championed the 'stationary state economy' and warned against the drive for unlimited economic growth.

concepts.name: Negative externalities
concepts.definition: Detrimental effects of an activity that go unrecognised, for which government intervention is justified.
concepts.supporting_text: Arthur C. Pigou … argued that when the detrimental effects of an activity went unrecognised, then the government should intervene. He described these detrimental effects as negative externalities.

concepts.name: Land economics (economics of the environment)
concepts.definition: A field of study that treats land and environmental services as economic factors, emerging only with contemporary environmentalism after earlier economic thought focused mainly on labour and capital.
concepts.supporting_text: As a consequence, land economics, or economics of the environment, did not develop fully into a field of its own until the emergence of contemporary environmentalism.

concepts.name: Environmental economics
concepts.definition: A field of study that examines the economic impacts of environmental policies and the value of natural resources, rooted in early economic theories that later influenced environmental thought.

concepts.name: Economic growth

concepts.name: Malthusian tradition
concepts.definition: A line of thought that emphasizes the risks of overpopulation and its potential to outstrip resource availability.
concepts.supporting_text: In the Malthusian tradition, many of these books focused on overpopulation.

concepts.name: Cowboy economy
concepts.definition: A metaphor for an open, unregulated economic system characterized by reckless, exploitative, romantic, and violent behaviour toward natural resources.
concepts.supporting_text: He called the open economy a 'cowboy' economy, symbolic of a cowboy's 'reckless, exploitative, romantic and violent behaviour'.

concepts.name: Spaceman economy

concepts.name: Open economy (as used by Boulding)

concepts.name: Population growth
concepts.definition: The increase in the number of people, highlighted as a major concern for planetary capacity and linked to environmental sustainability.

concepts.name: IPAT equation
concepts.definition: A simple mathematical concept that expresses environmental impact (I) as the product of three major determinants: population (P), affluence (A), and technology (T).

concepts.name: Limits to Growth
concepts.definition: A concept asserting that continued exponential growth in population, industrialization, pollution, food production, and resource depletion will reach planetary limits within a century, leading to a sudden and uncontrollable decline in both population and industrial capacity.
concepts.supporting_text: The Club's first report, The Limits to Growth (1972), was underpinned by the work of a group of systems scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), who had developed the first integrated global model linking the world economy and the environment. ... concepts.name: spaceship Earth metaphor
concepts.definition: A metaphor used to make the resource limitations of the economic system understandable to the wider public.
concepts.supporting_text: Boulding's use of the spaceship Earth metaphor made the resource limitations of the economic system understandable to the wider public.

concepts.name: entropy law (as applied to economics)
concepts.definition: The principle that whenever energy is used, the amount of usable energy available to society declines, based on the second law of thermodynamics.

concepts.name: bioeconomic programme
concepts.definition: An academic programme emphasizing the importance of viable technologies that can maintain economic activity over the long term without using irreplaceable resources.
concepts.supporting_text: Georgescu‑Roegen went on to dedicate his academic career to developing what he called a bioeconomic programme.

concepts.name: appropriate technology
concepts.definition: The use of technology that is suitable to scale and context, treating natural resources as capital rather than expandable income.

concepts.name: natural capital
concepts.definition: The concept that natural resources should be treated as capital, not as expandable income, implying they provide a dividend rather than being endlessly mined.

concepts.name: steady‑state economy (SSE)

concepts.name: sustainable economic welfare index
concepts.definition: An index constructed to replace GNP as a measure of economic wellbeing, intended to reflect sustainable economic welfare.
concepts.supporting_text: Daly and John B. Cobb (b. 1925) constructed an index of sustainable economic welfare intended to replace GNP as a measure of economic wellbeing.

concepts.name: ecological footprint
concepts.definition: A measure applied to national economies that quantifies the amount of biologically productive land and water area required to support a population’s consumption.
concepts.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

concepts.name: genuine progress indicator
concepts.definition: An alternative metric to GDP that attempts to account for environmental and social factors in assessing economic progress.
concepts.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

concepts.name: happy planet index
concepts.definition: An alternative indicator that combines well‑being, life expectancy and ecological footprint to assess national progress.
concepts.supporting_text: Measures such as the ecological footprint, genuine progress indicator and happy planet index have been applied to national economies...

concepts.name: sustainable development
concepts.definition: A broad idea linking economic progress with environmental stewardship, underpinning many alternative measures of economic wellbeing.
concepts.supporting_text: many linked to the idea of sustainable development.

concepts.name: Ecological economics
concepts.definition: A field that seeks to ensure the environment is recognised in standard economic theory and to set out an alternative to a capitalist (or communist) economic system by attributing monetary value to the environment and demonstrating the cost of its destruction.
concepts.supporting_text: Ecological economics is as much about ensuring the environment is recognised in standard economic theory as setting out an alternative to a capitalist (or communist) economic system. concepts.name: Cost‑benefit analysis
concepts.definition: A methodological tool widely used to make the case for environmental protection and to choose between different environmental protection options, though its application can be complex, controversial, and not always trusted by environmental campaigners or regulated industries.
concepts.supporting_text: Cost‑benefit analysis has been widely used to make the case for environmental protection and to choose between different environmental protection options. concepts.name: Social cost‑benefit analysis

concepts.name: Ecosystem services
concepts.definition: A conceptual framework that relates the functioning of ecosystems to the provision of services for humanity, categorised into provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting services, and used to translate ecological functions into economic language that highlights their human utility and value.
concepts.supporting_text: An approach to communicating this in a structured way has its origins in the 1970s, when the functioning of ecosystems was related to the provision of services... concepts.name: Environmental services
concepts.definition: An early term describing nine 'environmental services' whose decline would follow damage to ecosystem functioning, forming a precursor to the modern ecosystem services concept.
key_proponents: MIT Study of Critical Environmental Problems
concepts.supporting_text: An 1970 MIT report of the Study of Critical Environmental Problems, entitled Man's Impact on the Global Environment: Assessment and Recommendations for Action, described nine 'environmental services' that would decline if the functioning of ecosystems were damaged.

concepts.name: Public service functions of the environment
concepts.definition: The idea that the environment provides public service functions, a framing used to argue for its protection and valuation.
concepts.supporting_text: Holdren and Ehrlich advocated this idea and in an article for American Scientist described the 'public service functions of the environment'.

concepts.name: Four categories of ecosystem services
concepts.definition: A classification within the ecosystem services framework that groups services into provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting categories, each contributing to human wellbeing.
concepts.supporting_text: It defined the four categories of ecosystem services that contribute to human wellbeing as: provisioning services, such as food; regulating services, such as filtration of pollutants and flood control; cultural services, such as recreation; and supporting services, such as soil formation and photosynthesis.

concepts.name: Market failure
concepts.definition: A situation where negative externalities are not recognised by the market system, leading to over‑use or degradation of environmental goods and requiring correction through policy instruments.
concepts.supporting_text: Following Pigou, these negative externalities should be regarded as market failures and corrected.

concepts.name: Negative externalities
concepts.definition: Costs imposed on third parties or the environment that are not reflected in market prices, causing the full cost of ecosystem degradation to be ignored.
concepts.supporting_text: Because many ecosystem services are not recognised in the market system, the full cost of their degradation is not considered.

concepts.name: Discount rate (in climate economics)
concepts.definition: A numerical factor used to convert future values into present values; low rates give greater weight to future generations, while high rates diminish the importance of long‑term impacts.

concepts.name: No net loss

concepts.supporting_text: some business sectors are exploring 'no net loss' or 'net positive impact' initiatives in which their impacts are offset by undertaking environmental activities of at least equal value.

concepts.name: Tragedy of the commons
concepts.definition: A theoretical framework describing how individual rational actors, each seeking to maximise personal gain from a shared resource, collectively over‑exploit that resource, leading to its depletion or ruin.
concepts.supporting_text: In 1967, Garrett Hardin (1915-2003) developed the notion of the 'tragedy of the commons' where he used the analogy of common grazing land to illustrate that sharing common resources leads to over‑use.

concepts.name: Mutual coercion mutually agreed upon
concepts.definition: A proposed solution to the tragedy of the commons that involves collectively imposed restrictions or regulations that are accepted by all users to prevent over‑exploitation.
concepts.supporting_text: His solution was 'mutual coercion mutually agreed upon'.

concepts.name: Carbon pricing

concepts.name: Privatisation of natural resources

concepts.name: Ecosystem services approach

concepts.name: Universal right to water and sanitation
concepts.definition: The principle that access to basic water and sanitation is a universal human right and should not be treated as a negotiable commodity.

concepts.name: Cooperative institutions for common‑pool resources
concepts.definition: Durable, cooperative institutions that are organised and governed by the resource users themselves, proposed as a way to resolve commons problems.

concepts.name: Global Green New Deal (GGND)

concepts.supporting_text: Following in his footsteps, UNEP instigated the Global Green New Deal (GGND) initiative in December 2008.

concepts.name: Green fiscal spending
concepts.definition: Policy recommendation that the world’s richest economies allocate a share of GDP (e.g., 1 % of global GDP) to environmental initiatives and adopt policy changes that support environmentally‑focused public spending.

concepts.name: Green economy
